attribution.note: Marcus's own words in his own Substack post. The lawyer quote just before it is a separate sentence and is not part of the claim.

semantics.note: The claim keeps his scope (LLM imitation used as a substitute for human action) and his absolute 'never know in advance'. It is a general observation that is somewhat rhetorical but can be tested.

contract.note: Reading 'never know in advance' as 'cannot dependably tell before the attempt' is a fair, ordinary reading. Limiting the period to 2025 up to publication was the evaluator's choice and is reasonable. He named no task class, no threshold and no error tolerance, so the result depends on interpretation.

evidence.note: Peer-reviewed PredictaBoard paper, available June 2025, before publication. Most prediction methods it tested were near random, and almost none worked at strict error thresholds. This supports limited predictability on benchmark Q&A. But some pairs did well at the 0.8 threshold, and the tests are not real substitution for human work.
Anthropic's own 2022 study, so a company disclosure from before the target period. It shows some advance self-prediction is possible, with poor calibration on new tasks. Context only.

reviews.rationale: e1 shows that LLM attempts both succeed and fail, and that the methods it tested predicted outcomes poorly, especially at strict thresholds. That fits the first part of the claim and points toward the second. But it covers a few methods on benchmark Q&A only, and the support condition says that is not enough to establish the categorical claim. Nothing in the packet shows dependable advance prediction either. The categorical part is not settled, so the outcome is unresolved.
